I am afraid getting polymerization at longer wavelengths is a big problem. I have managed to get a result with pulsed Ruby at 694nm using ordinary

methylene blue (MB). From a paper in the 1970 by Andrejs Graube of Huges Aircraft Corp , he used methylene green (MG) which has a nitro group added to MB

this could take it too over 700nm. I tried it , and found it did not seem to work better at 694 nm than straight MB. MG is available from Aldrich as a zinc chloride salt

Jeff

I don't know if this will work for you but here is a dye that works for epoxy systems, apparently dissolved in chloroform: 

[http://www.epolin.com/index.cfm?act=cat ... talogid=84](http://www.epolin.com/index.cfm?act=catalog.cfm&catalogid=84)

It is on the Epolin site, which I have been looking at for my own purposes. They have a large range of dyes for the IR, with different solubilities, for laser absorption. This one peaks right where you want it.

Hey thanks for that tip Bill. 

I am fascinated to see the dye in question is anthraquinone . I have always thought of that one as a UV polymerization initiator. Is it possible it could have a double life down in the 756nm region I wonder. ---Things are usually not that simple. I think the problem comes down to the basic energy behind the light in question. There is a famous little equation about this E = hv where v= the light's frequency and h = Plancks constant.

Translated I think this means NIR light does'nt have enough oomph to break chemical bonds and create radicals. It is not actinic enough.

Another aspect is that if you do have a responsive system as in silver halide "NIR film" you get trouble from noise from thermal photons needing one to work at reduced temperatures .

Jeff

posts.topic_title: Any idea on near IR dye for photopolymer
posts.author: walschuler
posts.post_subject: Any idea on near IR dye for photopolymer
posts.content_md:
Jeff-

I was careful to say I don't know if this will work, and I realize the dyes on this site are blocking dyes for laser beam safety. So I don't know if it will link with a silver halide, and If it does I don't know if a photon at 1 micron or so will contribute enough energy to contribute electrons to a latent image. But commercial films do run out to almost 700nm with commercial sensitizers, and I don't see this as a big step in energy. 

Note this is not the thermal IR at 10 microns, so I doubt cooling will be necessary. I don't think one normally shoots commercial near-IR films with chilling. 

I may try to resensitize some film with the Epolite to try the idea out, anyhow.

I am going to reiterate what I said above based on the following:

Take a look at [http://photo.net/learn/optics/edscott/ir000020.htm](http://photo.net/learn/optics/edscott/ir000020.htm)

You will see senstivity curves for Kodak HS IR and Konica 750 film. The former has nearly uniform sensitivity out to about 925nm and the latter a hump that peaks at about 750nm. Both are silver halide films. So, Jeff, until you can make your photon energy argument stronger, perhaps show there is an excitation energy edge at, say, 950nm that prevents latent image electrons from being created in silver halide I wil continue to think there is a dye out there that will do the trick. 

For polymers it may well be another matter. I now realize I gave a chloroform soluble dye from Epolin, but what was asked for was water soluble. Epolin has those too. In fact for the original question of the exposure at 763nm, either of the above sensitizing systems might do as they must be water soluble. But you need to get the dye and the problem is both are likely trade secrets and not obtainable from the film makers. But there are specialist dye makers who subcontract to Kodak et al who have a huge range of dyes. The added problem is that in my experience it is tough to get them to supply sensitvity curves. But who knows??? If you want a supplier name, ask me and I will look for one this weekend. It came up in my Lippmann photography work some time ago.

Hello Viswanath,

Sorry for the delay in replying, but I have had to do more research and the sources I have been asking have been slow in replying. 

So far, I think your best bet is to try a company in the US called HW Sands, located in Jupiter, Florida. Their phone number is -for you- 001-561-743-8090, and they are on eastern standard time. The URL is:

[http://www.hwsands.com](http://www.hwsands.com). HW Sands is a large supplier of dyes, which used to do mostly visible photosensitizing dyes, but now does mostly IR photosensitizing dyes. Under the wavelength range of 751-775nm, they have several dyes that have absorptivities over 200 that might be useful to you. These include:#SDA 7590, abs max at 759nm, peak abs. 373 L/gm/cm, solvent methanol; SDA 2009, abs max at 761nm, abs 351 units, solvent methanol; SDB 5491, abs max 774nm, Abs units 369, solvent methanol, and also SDB 6906, abs max at 774nm, abs 409 units, solvent methanol. I know that the solvent is wrong but they tell me they can easily modify the dyes to be water soluble and are confident that they can be used to sensitize acrylamides. The web pages show absorption curves for each of their products. 

They are fairly expensive: at 1 gm quantity they charge around $US 150/gm, at 10 gms about $US 50/gm, and at 1 kg they charge about $US 5-10/gm.

You can email MIke Sovich at mikesovich at hwsands dot com and use my name..we are continuing to talk...

Bill Alschuler
